raw_response:
I'm a 38-year-old farmer in Xichengmeng, Houcun Township, Quzhou County. I graduated from Hebei Agricultural University with a degree in agricultural management, and I've been back on the farm for five years now. My family has four people — my wife, my parents, and me — but with 220 mu under management, we couldn't survive without machinery and hired labor. I own a rotary tiller and a precision planter, and I contract harvester crews at peak season. My wife handles procurement and bookkeeping.

I split my land roughly evenly: **110 mu of spring soybean** and **110.1 mu of millet** (huangjinmiao variety). I chose this split because the local oil processing plant gives me a stable purchase contract for soybean at about 2.5 yuan/kg, and the huangjinmiao millet fetches a premium from health-food buyers in Handan at 2.2 yuan/kg. Growing both insulates me if one market drops. Last year my millet yielded about 800 kg/mu and my soybean about 450 kg/mu. I'm targeting the same this year — I don't chase maximum yields because the marginal input cost isn't worth it at current prices.

For planting, I'll sow both crops around **April 20th**. I monitor soil temperature at 5 cm depth; once it holds above 10°C for three consecutive days, I know it's safe for soybean. I do a light **rotary tillage** first to break the surface crust, then machine sowing. The soybean seed rate is about 7 jin/mu (3.5 kg/mu), and the millet is only 1 jin/mu (0.5 kg/mu) because the seeds are tiny and the huangjinmiao variety costs about 50 yuan/mu.

For fertilizer, I base my rates on soil tests I paid for two years ago. I use a **balanced 15-15-15 compound fertilizer** applied entirely as basal at sowing — no topdressing. The millet gets **50 kg/mu** because it's a heavier feeder, especially for phosphorus and potassium. The soybean gets **40 kg/mu** — as a legume, it fixes most of its own nitrogen, and I've learned that pushing more N just causes lodging and reduces nodulation. I used to calculate exact NPK splits, but honestly, the compound is simpler, the price is predictable, and the results are consistent.

For irrigation, I pump from my well. Water is reliable but electricity isn't cheap — about 20 yuan/mu per irrigation. I budget **one irrigation for soybean at the flowering stage** (critical for pod set) and **one for millet at the booting stage** in mid-summer. The millet can survive dry spells, but that booting irrigation is what determines grain fill. I might skip it if July brings good rains, but I'm planning for one.

For pest management, my millet fields get weedy with chenopodium, so I'll spray **herbicide twice**. For soybean, I'll do **one insecticide spray at pod-filling** to control pod borers. I don't use fungicide unless I see disease during my weekly scouting — and I haven't needed it the past two years.

Labor is tight with only four of us. My family handles supervision, irrigation scheduling, and input delivery — about **5 days per mu** across the season. I hire labor for harvest, spraying, and some tillage — roughly **15 days per mu** total. At 220 mu, that's a lot of hired hands, but it's the only way to get the work done in the narrow windows.

My total input cost this season should run about **42,000 yuan**. I need to keep cash ready because the seed and fertilizer dealers want payment in March, and the harvest crews want cash on the day.
